title: Federated learning: training without moving the data
summary: FedAvg worked through on three clients, compression and server optimizers, drift and its fixes, personalization, attacks, secure aggregation, DP, and a real non-IID Flower run.
outcomes: Explain why the data cannot be centralized and write the federated objective as a weighted sum of per-client losses
Compute a FedAvg round by hand: local updates on three clients and the average weighted by sample count
Cut a round's cost with local work, unbiased compression and a server optimizer, and say what each cannot fix
Predict how label skew drifts FedAvg to a biased fixed point, and show how FedProx damps it and SCAFFOLD removes it
Choose between one global model, personalization, asynchronous FL and vertical FL for a given deployment
Recover an input from a linear layer's update, and compare median, trimmed mean, Krum and clipping against a poisoned client
Describe what a server sees under secure aggregation, and compute a clipped, noised DP-FedAvg round

lessons.title: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device

blocks.md:
You already know the centralized recipe: collect a dataset, compute the average loss over it, and walk the parameters downhill with gradient descent. Federated learning keeps that objective and throws away the collection step.

The motivating case is a phone keyboard. Everything you type is exactly the data that would improve next-word prediction, and it is exactly the data you would least like uploaded. Gboard, Google's keyboard app for phones, trained a next-word model this way on real phones: about 1.4 million parameters, 3000 rounds, data from 1.5 million users, with each round taking two to three minutes of wall-clock time. The same shape appears across organizations rather than devices: hospitals or banks that each hold records they are not permitted to pool.

Three obvious approaches fail, each for its own reason.

1. **Upload the raw data.** Often blocked by policy or law, and the raw logs are usually much bigger than the model you want to train.
2. **Train on one device alone.** A single phone holds a few hundred examples of one person's typing. That model overfits its owner and never sees the vocabulary of everyone else.
3. **Send a gradient every step.** Mathematically clean, and it is the baseline called FedSGD, but each step costs a network round trip to a phone on home wifi. FedSGD stands for federated stochastic gradient descent: each selected client computes one gradient on its local data, and the server averages those gradients and takes a single step. Reaching 99 percent on a small image model this way took 626 rounds in the original experiments, where a smarter scheme took 18. Those numbers are test accuracy on handwritten digits, from the 2017 paper by McMahan and colleagues at Google that coined the term federated learning; the smarter scheme is its federated averaging algorithm, FedAvg, which lesson 2 works through.

blocks.tex: f(w) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{n_k}{n} F_k(w), \qquad F_k(w) = \frac{1}{n_k} \sum_{i \in P_k} \ell(w; x_i, y_i)
blocks.caption: The federated objective. Client k holds the example set P_k of size n_k, F_k is its average loss over those examples (l is the loss on one example), and n is the total over all K clients. This equals the pooled average loss with the bookkeeping split up. Clients with more data pull harder.

blocks.md: The defining property is not cryptography. It is that **the data stays put and only parameters move**. In the standard description of the setting, a central orchestration server organizes the training but never sees raw data.

blocks.title: Three ways to use data that lives on phones

scenes.caption: Option 1: ship the raw examples to a datacenter and train normally. This is the approach that privacy policy, regulation and upload bandwidth all rule out.
Option 2: let each phone train only on itself. Phone A has 54 examples of one person's typing, so the model it learns is both tiny and personal to the point of useless for everyone else.
The federated round, step 1: the server selects some clients and broadcasts the current global model to each of them. The datacenter copy of the data never exists.
Step 2: each selected client runs several local epochs of ordinary SGD on its own examples, starting from the broadcast model. The examples never leave the box they are in.
Step 3: only parameters travel back, and the server averages them weighted by how many examples each client trained on. One round is done; now repeat a few thousand times.

blocks.md:
Two regimes get used in practice, and they differ in almost every systems dimension.

**Cross-device**: the clients are phones or IoT (internet of things) devices such as sensors and smart home gadgets. The population runs up to $10^{10}$ clients, only a fraction are reachable at any moment with a strong day and night cycle, clients cannot be addressed individually, they are stateless (a client usually participates once and never again), and 5 percent or more of a round's clients are expected to fail or drop out mid-round.

**Cross-silo**: the clients are typically 2 to 100 organizations or geo-distributed datacenters. They are stateful, addressable, almost always available, and failures are rare. Communication may or may not be the bottleneck.

Typical orders of magnitude for a cross-device application: 50 to 5000 devices selected per round, $10^5$ to $10^7$ devices touched over the life of a model, 500 to 10000 rounds, and 1 to 10 days of wall-clock training.

blocks.prompt: You have 100 phones, each with 600 examples, and you can afford 100 network round trips total. Would you rather spend each round trip on one gradient step from every phone, or on each phone doing a few hundred local steps?
blocks.reveal: Local steps, by a wide margin, and this is the whole design. In the original MNIST experiments the one-gradient-per-round scheme (FedSGD) needed 626 rounds to hit 99 percent, while letting each client run 20 local epochs with batch size 10 needed 18 rounds for the same accuracy. MNIST is a standard dataset of 70000 small grayscale images of handwritten digits, 60000 of them for training; the paper split those 60000 across 100 clients, 600 each, which is where this question's numbers come from. You have no budget problem on the devices (they are idle and charging), and a severe budget problem on the network. Lesson 3 quantifies exactly when this trade stops working.

blocks.question: Eight hospitals want one shared model and no record may leave any hospital. What is the training objective?
options: Each hospital trains alone and the best of the eight models is shipped
The same pooled average loss as centralized training, written as a sum of per-hospital losses weighted by record count
The unweighted mean of the eight per-hospital losses, since each hospital is one client
A new objective that no centralized training run could express
blocks.explain: Federated learning changes who computes, not what is being minimized. The objective is the pooled average loss, which factors exactly into a sum over clients with weights n_k/n. The unweighted mean is a different objective: it would give a hospital with 200 records the same influence as one with 20000.

blocks.question: In cross-device federated learning, which expectation is realistic for a single round?
options: Every device in the population contributes once per round
The same few hundred devices are reused every round so they can carry state
A few hundred devices are chosen from the much larger set currently available, and some of them will not report back
Devices are addressed by identifier so the server can retry a specific one
blocks.explain: Availability is the constraint. Tens of thousands of devices may be checking in, the server picks a few hundred, clients are not individually addressable and are treated as stateless, and 5 percent or more of a round's participants are expected to drop out. Carrying per-client state across rounds is a cross-silo luxury.

lessons.title: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds

blocks.md:
FedAvg is four lines. The server keeps a model $w_t$. Each round it samples a fraction $C$ of the $K$ clients, sends them $w_t$, and each selected client runs $E$ epochs of plain SGD over its local data with minibatch size $B$ and learning rate $\eta$, then sends back the parameters it ended up with. The server replaces $w_t$ with a weighted average of those parameter vectors, weighting client k by how many examples it trained on.

That is it. No gradients are sent, no data is sent, and the only thing the algorithm knows about a client is its parameter vector and its sample count.

blocks.code:
# Algorithm 1 of McMahan et al. 2017, written as Python
def federated_averaging(K, C, E, B, eta, rounds):
    w = init_model()
    for t in range(rounds):
        m = max(int(C * K), 1)
        S = sample_clients(m)                   # server picks who trains
        results = []
        for k in S:                             # in parallel, on devices
            results.append((n[k], client_update(k, w, E, B, eta)))
        m_t = sum(n_k for n_k, _ in results)    # examples in THIS round
        w = sum((n_k / m_t) * w_k for n_k, w_k in results)
    return w

def client_update(k, w, E, B, eta):
    for epoch in range(E):
        for batch in split(local_data[k], B):
            w = w - eta * grad_loss(w, batch)
    return w                                    # parameters, not data
blocks.caption: B set to the whole local dataset means one full-batch step per epoch. The paper writes that case as B equal to infinity.

blocks.tex: w_{t+1} = \sum_{k \in S_t} \frac{n_k}{m_t} w_{t+1}^{k}, \qquad m_t = \sum_{k \in S_t} n_k
blocks.caption: The aggregation step. S_t is the set of clients that reported in round t and m_t is their total example count, so the weights sum to one over this round only; an erratum in the paper corrected an earlier version that divided by the full n.

blocks.md: Three knobs control the cost. $C$ is the fraction of clients per round, and the experiments settle on $C = 0.1$ as a good balance. $E$ is the number of local epochs and $B$ the local minibatch size; together they set how much work a client does before it is allowed to talk. The expected number of SGD updates a client performs per round is

blocks.caption: Local updates per client per round, and its expectation over a uniformly drawn client. With 600 examples per client, E equal to 20 and B equal to 10, one client does 1200 SGD steps between two network messages.

blocks.md:
Now real arithmetic. The toy problem is a one-parameter least squares fit: the model predicts $\hat{y} = w x$ and the loss on one point is $\frac{1}{2}(w x - y)^2$, half the squared error so the derivative carries no stray 2. There are 108 points of three kinds, and three clients.

- Client A holds 54 copies of $(x, y) = (1, 1)$
- Client B holds 36 copies of $(x, y) = (2, 4)$
- Client C holds 18 copies of $(x, y) = (3, 9)$

Each client's loss is a parabola in $w$, with its own minimum $\mu_k$ and its own curvature $a_k$. The script that produced every number below computes them as exact fractions: $\mu = 1, 2, 3$ and $a = 1, 4, 9$. The weights are $p_k = n_k/n = 1/2, 1/3, 1/6$, and the minimum of the pooled objective is $w^{*} = 2.3$ exactly.

Here is where those numbers come from. On one client every point is the same $(x, y)$, so its average loss is half the square of $wx - y$. Pulling $x$ out of the bracket rewrites that as $x^2/2$ times the square of $w - y/x$. The curvature $a_k$ is the factor $x^2$ in front (in general, the mean of $x^2$ over the client's points), and the minimum sits where the bracket is zero, at $\mu_k = y/x$. Client A gives $a = 1$ and $\mu = 1$. Client B has $x = 2$ and $y = 4$, so its loss is half the square of $2w - 4$, which is 2 times the square of $w - 2$: $a = 4$ and $\mu = 2$. Client C gives $a = 9$ and $\mu = 3$.

The pooled loss is $\sum_k p_k \frac{a_k}{2}(w - \mu_k)^2$ plus a constant. Setting its derivative to zero gives $w^{*} = \sum_k p_k a_k \mu_k / \sum_k p_k a_k$, a curvature-weighted average of the local optima. In sixths that is $(3 + 16 + 27)/(3 + 8 + 9) = 46/20 = 2.3$.

blocks.caption: Local full-batch gradient step for this problem, with a_k the mean of x squared on client k and mu_k its local optimum. We use eta = 0.1, which keeps every client stable since eta times a_k stays below 1.

blocks.md: The gradient of that loss is $a_k(w - \mu_k)$, so one step moves the client a fraction $\eta a_k$ of the way from $w$ to $\mu_k$: 0.1 of the gap for A, 0.4 for B, 0.9 for C. Keeping $\eta a_k$ below 1 means no client overshoots its own optimum. From $w = 0$ the clients land at 0.1 x 1 = 0.10, 0.4 x 2 = 0.80 and 0.9 x 3 = 2.70.

blocks.prompt: Start from w = 0 and let every client take one local step (E = 1, B = full batch). Client A ends at 0.10, client B at 0.80, client C at 2.70. What does the server set as the new global model?
blocks.reveal:
Not 1.20, which is the plain mean of the three. Weighting by sample count gives

0.5 x 0.10 + (1/3) x 0.80 + (1/6) x 2.70 = 0.050 + 0.267 + 0.450 = **0.766667**

And there is a second, sharper surprise: 0.766667 is exactly what one full-batch gradient step on all 108 pooled points gives. With E = 1 and full participation, FedAvg is not an approximation of centralized gradient descent; it is centralized gradient descent, rearranged.

blocks.title: The weighted average, cell by cell

scenes.caption: Round 1 starts. The server broadcasts w = 0 to all three clients. Sample counts are fixed properties of the clients and are sent back with the update.
Each client takes one local full-batch step toward its own optimum. Client C has the steepest loss (a = 9), so it moves furthest: from 0 to 2.70, nearly all the way to its local optimum of 3.
The server computes the weights. m_t is 108 here because all three clients reported, so the weights are 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108.
Multiply and sum: 0.050 plus 0.267 plus 0.450 is 0.766667. Client C moved ten times further than client A but carries one third of its weight, so the big quiet client dominates.
Round 2 from w = 0.766667. The clients return 0.79, 1.26 and 2.776667, and the weighted average is 1.277778, which again matches a second full-batch gradient step on the pooled data exactly.

blocks.title: Two rounds of FedAvg on three clients

scenes.caption: Round 1, broadcast. Every client starts this round from the same global model, w = 0. That shared starting point is what makes averaging their results sane at all.
Round 1, local training. Each client walks toward its own optimum (1, 2 and 3), at a speed set by its own curvature.
Round 1, aggregation. The weighted average lands at 0.766667, below all but one client, because the largest client wants the smallest slope.
Round 2, broadcast. The clients forget their own round-1 models completely and restart from the server's. Nothing but the global model survives a round boundary.
Round 2, local training. The gaps between clients are smaller now, since they all start closer to their own optima than they did at w = 0.
Round 2, aggregation: 1.277778. Two rounds have covered a bit over half the distance to the optimum of 2.3, and that is with every client reporting every round.

blocks.md: A common misreading is that FedAvg averages the clients' answers. It averages their **parameters**. In this problem the sample-weighted average of the three local optima is 1.667 and the plain average is 2.0, while the true optimum is 2.3. Averaging models that have fully solved their own problems gives the wrong model.

With $E = 1$, full batches and full participation, FedAvg is exactly full-batch gradient descent on the pooled objective. Everything interesting about federated optimization, good and bad, comes from doing more than one local step.

blocks.question: Client A (54 examples) returns 0.10, client B (36) returns 0.80, client C (18) returns 2.70, but this round client B drops out and never reports. What does FedAvg set as the new global model?
options: 0.767, since the weights 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108 are properties of the clients
0.500, the weighted average with client B's contribution set to zero
0.750, the weighted average of A and C renormalized over 72 examples
The round is discarded, because FedAvg requires every selected client
blocks.explain: The denominator is m_t, the examples in this round only: 54 + 18 = 72. So the model is (54/72) x 0.10 + (18/72) x 2.70 = 0.075 + 0.675 = 0.750. Keeping stale weights that sum to less than one (option B) would shrink the model toward zero, and single dropouts never abandon a round.

blocks.question: A client has 800 local examples. You set E = 4 and B = 20. How many SGD updates does it perform per round, and how many parameter vectors does it send?
options: 40 updates, 4 vectors (one per epoch)
160 updates, 1 vector
800 updates, 1 vector
4 updates, 1 vector
blocks.explain: Updates per round are E times n_k divided by B, so 4 x 800 / 20 = 160 steps. All of that local work produces exactly one message: the parameters the client holds when the last epoch ends. That asymmetry between local compute and network traffic is the reason FedAvg exists.

lessons.title: Buying rounds with local work, and when that stops working

blocks.md:
A round costs bytes on a consumer uplink, and it costs minutes of wall-clock time while the server waits. So the metric that matters is rounds to target accuracy, not epochs or examples seen.

Take the convolutional neural network (CNN) from the original paper, an image model whose early layers slide small learned filters across the picture: two 5x5 convolution layers, a 512-unit dense (fully connected) layer, 1663370 parameters. At 4 bytes per parameter (one 32-bit floating point number each) that is 6.65 MB of model, which every selected client downloads and (roughly) uploads again each round. With $C = 0.1$ over 100 clients, 10 clients participate, so one round moves about 66.5 MB of updates up to the server. The question is how many such rounds you need.

The two scenes split the same 60000 MNIST training images over 100 clients in two ways. Independent and identically distributed (IID) means every client's examples are drawn at random from the same overall distribution, so each client looks like a small copy of the whole dataset. Here that means shuffle, then deal 600 images to each client. Non-IID is any split where that fails, so clients see different mixes of the data. The pathological non-IID split is the deliberately extreme one: sort by digit label, cut into 200 shards of 300 images, and give each client two shards, so most clients see only two of the ten digits.

blocks.title: Rounds to 99 percent on MNIST, by how much local work per round

scenes.caption: IID split (data shuffled, 600 examples per client). One gradient step per round needs 626 rounds. Adding local work collapses that to 18 rounds, a 34.8x saving, and it is mostly driven by the smaller batch size.

Pathological non-IID split: data sorted by label, cut into 200 shards of 300, two shards per client, so most clients see only two digits. Every FedAvg setting needs far more rounds, and E=5 with full batches needs 1000, worse than sending single gradients.

blocks.md:
Read the two scenes together. On the IID split the trade is almost free: 626 rounds become 18, so the total upload to reach 99 percent falls from about 41.6 GB to about 1.2 GB (626 x 10 x 6.65 MB against 18 x 10 x 6.65 MB). Meanwhile the local work per client per round goes from 1 SGD update to 1200. You spent device compute, which is idle and free, to buy network rounds, which are scarce.

On the pathological non-IID split the same settings need 173 rounds instead of 18. The saving is real but an order of magnitude smaller, and one setting (E = 5 with full local batches, 1000 rounds) is twice as slow as just sending gradients.

blocks.title: More local work from bigger E or smaller B, same bytes per round

scenes.caption: B = 600 is the whole local dataset: one update per epoch, so u = E. Ten local epochs is ten gradient steps, and the client still uploads one 6.65 MB model.

B = 50 multiplies the updates by 12 at no communication cost at all. The paper's advice is to tune B down first, because lowering it is nearly free as long as B stays large enough to saturate the device's hardware.
B = 10, E = 20: 1200 updates per client per round, against one single update for FedSGD. The upload curve has not moved. That gap is the entire resource argument for FedAvg.

blocks.md: So why not set $E$ to 1000? Because local work is only useful while the local objectives agree with the global one, and past some point extra local steps move a client toward its own optimum rather than everyone's.

The evidence in the original paper is uneven in an instructive way. On the MNIST convolutional model, large $E$ showed no significant degradation. On a character-level LSTM trained on Shakespeare roles, large numbers of local epochs made FedAvg plateau or diverge. Long short-term memory (LSTM) is a recurrent network design: it reads text one character at a time and carries a learned memory forward from step to step. The Shakespeare data gives each speaking role in each play its own client, so the clients are naturally non-IID. On a large-scale next-word model over more than 500000 authors, $E = 1$ was slightly better than $E = 5$. The paper's suggestion is to decay local computation late in training, the way you decay a learning rate.

blocks.prompt: Your federated run converges steadily at E = 1 and you want it twice as fast, so you set E = 10. Rounds to your accuracy target get worse, not better. What is the most likely cause?
blocks.reveal: The clients disagree. With heterogeneous data, ten local epochs take each client most of the way to its own optimum, and the average of those models is not the model that minimizes the pooled loss. You are converging quickly to the wrong point. Lesson 5 computes that wrong point exactly on our three-client problem: E = 1 lands on 2.3, E = 5 lands on 1.944, and large E approaches 1.667.

blocks.question: You halve B and keep E fixed. Which quantity changes the most?
options: Bytes uploaded per client per round, which doubles
SGD updates per client per round, which doubles
Rounds to the accuracy target, which always halves
The number of clients the server must wait for
blocks.explain: Updates per round are E times n_k over B, so halving B doubles them. Communication per round is set by the model size, not by B or E: one download and one upload of the parameters. Whether the extra local work converts into fewer rounds depends on how heterogeneous the clients are, so option C is exactly the trap.

blocks.question: In the original experiments, which result shows that more local computation is not always better?
options: On the IID MNIST split, E = 20 with B = 10 needed 18 rounds instead of 626
The model reached a higher final accuracy (99.44 percent) than the gradient-averaging baseline
A client fraction of C = 0.1 worked about as well as C = 1.0
On the non-IID split, E = 5 with full local batches needed 1000 rounds while single gradients needed 483
blocks.explain: That row is the one setting in the table slower than the FedSGD baseline, a 0.5x speedup. It is the fingerprint of local work pulling clients apart. The Shakespeare LSTM shows the same effect more dramatically: with very large E, training can plateau or diverge.

lessons.title: Cheaper rounds and smarter servers: compression and FedOpt

blocks.md:
Lesson 3 bought fewer rounds with more local work. This lesson attacks the other two factors: the bytes each round moves, and what the server does with the updates once they arrive.

Start from the same model: the 1663370-parameter CNN is 6.65 MB at 32 bits per parameter, and each of the 10 clients in a round uploads that much. Upload is the slow direction on consumer networks. The compression paper below quotes US averages of 55.0 Mbps down and 18.9 Mbps up (speedtest.net, 2016), so one 6.65 MB update takes about 2.8 seconds to send and about 1.0 second to receive. Secure aggregation (lesson 9) adds further upload bytes on top.

Konečný, McMahan and colleagues at Google (2016) proposed two families of uplink savers.

- **Structured updates** restrict the update to a smaller space while training. *Low rank*: the update matrix is $H = AB$ with $A$ random (regenerated from a seed) and only $B$ trained and sent. *Random mask*: a seed fixes a random sparsity pattern and the client sends only the non-zero values plus the seed.
- **Sketched updates** train the full update, then compress it lossily before sending: *subsampling* (send a random scaled subset), *probabilistic quantization* (below), and a *random rotation* applied first so that quantization error spreads evenly.

In their CIFAR-10 experiments (60000 small colour images in 10 classes) random masks beat low rank, and the combined methods cut total communication by two orders of magnitude.

blocks.tex: \tilde h_j = \begin{cases} h_{\max} & \text{with probability } \dfrac{h_j - h_{\min}}{h_{\max} - h_{\min}} \\[4pt] h_{\min} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad \mathbb{E}[\tilde h_j] = h_j
blocks.caption: One-bit probabilistic quantization of an update vector h: every coordinate becomes the vector's max or min, at random, with the probability chosen so its expected value is exact. 32x smaller than a 4-byte float; b bits per value repeats the trick inside 2^b intervals.

blocks.prompt: A client's update has four coordinates: -0.20, 0.05, 0.15 and 0.60 (mean 0.15). With one bit per value, each coordinate becomes either the min (-0.20) or the max (0.60). Why not simply round each one to the nearer of the two?
blocks.reveal:
Because rounding to the nearer end is biased, and the server averages thousands of these. Nearest rounding sends -0.20, -0.20, -0.20, 0.60, whose mean is 0.00 instead of 0.15, and every client with a similar shape errs in the same direction, so the errors add up instead of cancelling.

Probabilistic rounding sends 0.05 as the max with probability 0.25/0.80 = 0.3125, and 0.15 as the max with probability 0.4375. Each coordinate is right on average. A script averaging 10000 random draws gets back -0.200, 0.050, 0.150, 0.600 to within 0.005. The noise is real, but it is zero-mean, and averaging over clients shrinks it.

blocks.title: One-bit quantization of four values: nearest versus probabilistic

scenes.caption: The update to send. Its min is -0.20 and its max is 0.60; with one bit per coordinate the client transmits those two floats once, then one bit per coordinate saying which end to use.
Deterministic: round each value to the nearer end. 0.05 and 0.15 both fall closer to -0.20. The mean drops from 0.15 to 0.00: a bias that repeats for every similar client.
Probabilistic: the chance of sending the max is the value's position between the ends, (h - min)/(max - min). The ends themselves are sent exactly.
Expected value of what is sent equals the original in every coordinate, so the server's average over many clients is unbiased. The price is variance, which the random rotation of the paper reduces.

blocks.title: Upload cost of the 6.65 MB CNN under each scheme

scenes.caption: Megabytes uploaded per client per round: 6.65, 1.66, 0.21 and 0.67. Simplified: ignores the two floats per layer that 1-bit and 8-bit schemes also send, the mask seed, and protocol overhead.
Per round with 10 clients: 66.5, 16.6, 2.1 and 6.7 MB reach the server. Lesson 3's 626-round FedSGD run at 1 bit would move about 1.3 GB instead of 41.6 GB.
Seconds per upload on an 18.9 Mbps uplink: 2.82, 0.70, 0.09 and 0.28. The device's compute is idle and free; these seconds are what the round waits on.

blocks.md: Compression is lossy, and lossy is only safe when it is **unbiased**. Probabilistic quantization and scaled subsampling are unbiased per client, so their errors average out across a round. A biased compressor (rounding to nearest, keeping only the largest entries) pushes every client the same way, which looks like drift in disguise.

Now the server. Reddi and colleagues at Google (2020) rewrote one FedAvg round as $x_{t+1} = x_t - 1 \cdot (-\Delta_t)$, where $\Delta_t$ is the average of the client deltas $x_i - x_t$. Read that way, FedAvg is plain SGD on the server, with the **pseudo-gradient** $-\Delta_t$ and a server learning rate of exactly 1. A pseudo-gradient is a vector used in place of a gradient although no loss was differentiated to get it.

Once the 1 is visible it becomes a knob, and the server can run any optimizer on the pseudo-gradient. The family is called **FedOpt**. Its members include **FedAvgM** (server momentum, proposed by Hsu and colleagues in 2019: keep $v \leftarrow \beta v + \Delta$ and step along $v$), **FedAdagrad**, **FedYogi** and **FedAdam**. The optimizer state lives only on the server, so clients do the same work and send the same bytes as in FedAvg.

blocks.tex: m_t = \beta_1 m_{t-1} + (1-\beta_1)\Delta_t, \quad v_t = \beta_2 v_{t-1} + (1-\beta_2)\Delta_t^2, \quad x_{t+1} = x_t + \eta \frac{m_t}{\sqrt{v_t} + \tau}
blocks.caption: FedAdam's server step (Reddi et al., Algorithm 2), coordinate by coordinate. eta is the server learning rate, beta_1 and beta_2 the moment decays, and tau a floor that sets how adaptive the step is: smaller tau, more adaptive.

blocks.title: Our three clients with a server learning rate s

scenes.caption: s = 1 is plain FedAvg, the curves of lesson 5. With E = 1 the model is within 0.01 of 2.3 from round 14; with E = 5 it settles on 1.944 by round 5.
s = 0.5 halves every server step: 30 rounds for E = 1 and 13 for E = 5. Neither curve moves its destination.
s = 1.45: 9 rounds for E = 1 and 2 for E = 5. A bigger server step speeds both runs up, and the E = 5 run still stops at 1.944, not 2.3.

blocks.md:
The numbers behind the figure come from the closed form of lesson 5: with E = 1 each round shrinks the gap to 2.3 by a factor $1 - s/3$. A script gives rounds until the model stays within 0.01 of 2.3, starting from 0:

- $s = 0.5$: 30 rounds; $s = 1$ (FedAvg): 14; $s = 2$: 5; $s = 3$: 1, because the factor is exactly 0 (the server step lands on the minimum); $s = 4$: 5 rounds, overshooting to 3.07 first.
- Server momentum at $s = 1$: $\beta = 0.2$ takes 8 rounds, $\beta = 0.5$ takes 16, and $\beta = 0.9$ overshoots to 4.1 and needs 101.

Momentum and adaptivity earn their keep on noisy, badly scaled problems with millions of coordinates and a few hundred sampled clients, which is where Hsu et al. and Reddi et al. measured their gains. On a deterministic one-parameter toy they mostly overshoot.

FedAvg is server SGD with learning rate 1 on the pseudo-gradient $-\Delta_t$. A server optimizer changes how fast and how smoothly the model moves along the averaged client delta. It cannot change where that delta points: the drifted fixed point of lesson 5 is a fixed point for every server optimizer, because there the averaged delta is zero.

blocks.question: Compared with FedAvg, which hyperparameter does FedAdam expose that FedAvg implicitly fixes at 1?
options: The client learning rate eta_l
The number of local epochs E
The server learning rate eta applied to the averaged client delta
The fraction of clients C sampled per round
blocks.explain: Written as FedOpt, FedAvg's server step is x plus 1 times the averaged delta. FedAdam replaces that with eta times m over (sqrt(v) + tau), adding beta_1, beta_2 and tau as well. The client learning rate, E and C exist in FedAvg already and keep their meaning.

blocks.question: On the skewed split with E = 5, a colleague replaces FedAvg with a well-tuned FedAdam and expects the toy to reach 2.3. Where does it converge, if it converges?
options: To 2.3, because adaptive steps correct client drift
To about 1.944, the same fixed point, because the averaged delta is zero there whatever the server does
To 1.667, the average of the local optima
It cannot converge, since Adam needs true gradients
blocks.explain: At 1.944 the clients' moves cancel in the weighted average, so the pseudo-gradient is zero and every server optimizer stops there. Server optimizers change speed and stability. To move the destination you must change what clients compute: less local work, a proximal term, or SCAFFOLD's control variates (lesson 5).

lessons.title: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer

blocks.md:
Non-IID in federated learning is not one phenomenon. The common forms are label skew (one user types in one language, one hospital sees one patient population), quantity skew (one client has 50 examples and another 50000), and feature skew (different sensors, different handwriting). The original paper built the extreme case on purpose: sort MNIST by digit, cut it into 200 shards of 300 examples, and give each of 100 clients 2 shards, so most clients only ever see two digits.

We can get the same effect on our three-client problem by resplitting the same 108 points two ways.

blocks.title: The same 108 points, split two ways

scenes.caption: Skewed split: each client holds exactly one kind of point. Local optima are 1, 2 and 3 and local curvatures are 1, 4 and 9, so the clients disagree about both the answer and how confident they are.
IID split of the identical 108 points: every client gets all three kinds in proportion to its size. Now every client has curvature 10/3 and local optimum 2.3, which is also the global optimum.
Column sums are unchanged (54, 36, 18 points of each kind) and so are the client sizes. Nothing about the data or the objective differs between the two scenes; only who holds what.

blocks.md: Run FedAvg from $w_0 = 0$ with $\eta = 0.1$ on both splits. Lesson 2 showed that each local step multiplies a client's distance to its own optimum by $1 - \eta a_k$, so $E$ steps multiply it by $1 - \eta a_k$ raised to the power $E$, which we call $r_k$. Because each local problem is a parabola, a client's model after $E$ full-batch steps has a closed form, which makes the whole trajectory exactly computable:

blocks.caption: Each client contracts toward its own optimum by a factor r_k per round: it ends at mu_k plus r_k times its starting gap. For eta = 0.1 and E = 5: r = 0.590, 0.078, 0.00001 for clients A, B and C (0.9, 0.6 and 0.1 to the fifth). Client C is already sitting on its local optimum when it reports.

blocks.title: IID versus label-skewed, same points, same E

scenes.caption: With E = 1, FedAvg is pooled gradient descent, so the split does not matter at all: both the IID and the skewed run follow this identical curve and reach 2.3 (within 0.01 by round 14).
IID with E = 5: five local steps per round instead of one, and the curve is within 0.01 of the optimum by round 3 instead of round 14. This is the free lunch lesson 3 promised.
Skewed with E = 5: fastest early progress of all three, then it flattens at 1.9439 and stays there forever. It converges, quickly, to a point that is not the optimum. That is client drift.

blocks.md: The flat line is not noise or a bad learning rate. The round map, the rule that turns this round's global model into the next one, is affine, so it has a fixed point, and we can write it down. Averaging the clients' closed forms gives $w_{t+1} = \sum_k p_k (1 - r_k)\mu_k + \left(\sum_k p_k r_k\right) w_t$. In words, the next model is a constant built from the clients' optima, plus the current model $w_t$ times the number $\sum_k p_k r_k$. A constant plus a fixed multiple is what affine means. A fixed point is a value the map sends to itself, so once the model lands there it never moves. Setting $w_{t+1} = w_t$ and solving gives the formula below. That multiple is below 1 (0.32 for $E = 5$), so every round shrinks the gap to the fixed point by that factor, and FedAvg converges there.

blocks.tex: w_{\infty} = \frac{\sum_k p_k (1 - r_k)\, \mu_k}{\sum_k p_k (1 - r_k)}, \qquad p_k = \frac{n_k}{n}, \quad r_k = (1-\eta a_k)^{E}
blocks.caption: Where FedAvg stops on this problem: a weighted average of the local optima, where client k's weight is p_k times 1 minus r_k, the share of its gap it closes per round. For E = 1, 1 minus r_k is exactly eta times a_k, restoring the curvature weighting and the true optimum. For E above 1 it does not.

blocks.md:
The computed fixed points on the skewed split, all with $\eta = 0.1$:

- $E = 1$: 2.300000, the exact optimum
- $E = 2$: 2.147887
- $E = 5$: 1.943889
- $E = 50$: 1.668389
- $E \to \infty$: 1.666667, which is exactly $\sum_k p_k \mu_k$, the weighted average of the local optima

That limit is the mechanism in one line. As local work grows, each client arrives at its own optimum, so the server averages optima instead of averaging gradients, and the average of the optima is not the optimum of the average. This is the client drift that the SCAFFOLD paper (Karimireddy and colleagues, 2020; the name stands for stochastic controlled averaging for federated learning) illustrates with exactly this argument: the server update moves toward the mean of the client optima rather than toward the global optimum. On the IID split every $\mu_k$ equals 2.3, so there is nothing to drift to and bigger $E$ is pure profit.

Two well-known corrections, both grounded in the same picture:

**FedProx** adds a proximal term to the local objective, which penalizes moving away from the broadcast model. The term is $\frac{\mu}{2}$ times the squared distance between the local model $w$ and the broadcast model $w_t$, written $\lVert w - w_t \rVert^2$: a quadratic penalty, and proximal just means keep close to. This $\mu$ is the penalty strength and has nothing to do with the local optima $\mu_k$ of our toy problem. FedProx also explicitly allows stragglers to send partial work (an inexact local solution) instead of being dropped. The paper reports improving absolute test accuracy by 22 percent on average in highly heterogeneous settings.

**SCAFFOLD** keeps a control variate $c_i$ per client and $c$ on the server, and corrects each local gradient by $c - c_i$ so that local steps point along the global descent direction rather than the local one.

A control variate is a correction term that estimates a known bias so it can be subtracted. Here $c_i$ estimates client $i$'s own gradient direction and $c$, the mean of the $c_i$, estimates the global one. Adding $c - c_i$ to a local gradient swaps the client's own pull for the population's pull, so many local steps no longer walk off toward the client's own optimum. In the formula below, $y_i$ is the client's local model, $g_i$ its stochastic gradient and $\eta_l$ the local learning rate.

blocks.tex: \min_w h_k(w; w_t) = F_k(w) + \frac{\mu}{2} \lVert w - w_t \rVert^2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad y_i \leftarrow y_i - \eta_l \left( g_i(y_i) + c - c_i \right)
blocks.caption: Left: the FedProx local objective, with mu = 0 recovering FedAvg. Right: one SCAFFOLD local step, where the control variates are initialized to zero and maintained so that c is the mean of the c_i.

blocks.md: On our toy problem, a proximal term with $\mu = 2$ moves the $E = 5$ fixed point from 1.944 to 1.995 and slows the first round from 1.320 to 0.988. It buys accuracy with speed, and it does not reach 2.3. Treat these methods as damping on drift, not as a cure; the honest cure for this toy is $E = 1$ or a control-variate correction, which the figure below runs.

Here is how SCAFFOLD keeps its control variates honest, using Karimireddy et al.'s cheaper Option II. After its $K$ local steps (here $K$ counts local steps, not clients), client $i$ sets its new variate from the distance it travelled: $c_i^{+} = c_i - c + (x - y_i)/(K\eta_l)$, where $x$ is the model it received and $y_i$ the model it ended with. The fraction $(x - y_i)/(K\eta_l)$ is the average corrected step it took; adding back $c_i - c$ removes the correction and leaves the average of the client's own gradients over its $K$ steps. The client uploads both $y_i - x$ and $c_i^{+} - c_i$, and the server moves $c$ by the average change. Before any training every variate is zero, and with all $c_i$ fixed at zero SCAFFOLD is exactly FedAvg.

blocks.tex: c_i^{+} = c_i - c + \frac{x - y_i}{K\eta_l}, \qquad x \leftarrow x + \eta_g \sum_{i} p_i (y_i - x), \qquad c \leftarrow c + \sum_{i} p_i (c_i^{+} - c_i)
blocks.caption: SCAFFOLD's round with full participation. The paper averages uniformly over sampled clients; we weight by p_i = n_i/n, as FedAvg does here, so that the target stays the pooled optimum 2.3. eta_g is a server learning rate, set to 1.

blocks.title: Skewed split, E = 5: FedAvg, FedProx and SCAFFOLD round by round

scenes.caption: FedAvg: within 0.01 of its fixed point by round 5, and that point is 1.944. Every later round repeats it.
FedProx with mu = 2: slower start (0.988 after round 1) and a better end, creeping toward 1.995. Damped, not cured.
SCAFFOLD, Option II: round 1 equals FedAvg (all variates start at 0), then the corrections kick in. 2.216 by round 3, and within 0.01 of 2.3 from round 9 on.

blocks.md:
The variates converge to something you can check by hand. After 15 rounds the script has $c_A, c_B, c_C$ = 1.299, 1.191 and -6.283, closing on 1.3, 1.2 and -6.3. Those are $a_k(2.3 - \mu_k)$, each client's own gradient at the optimum, and their weighted mean $c$ goes to 0, the pooled gradient at the optimum. Adding $c - c_i$ to every local step cancels exactly the pull toward the client's own optimum.

The price: each client uploads twice as much (model delta plus variate delta), and each client must keep $c_i$ between rounds. That suits cross-silo federations, where the same few organizations take part every round, and fits poorly with stateless phones that may participate once.

Simplified model: ours is one parameter, convex, deterministic, full-batch and fully participating. Real drift in a deep network is worse and messier (it interacts with batch normalization statistics, the per-feature means and variances a normalization layer estimates from each client's own data; with momentum, the running average of past steps an optimizer keeps; and with client sampling), but the direction of the error is the one computed here.

blocks.question: On the skewed split with E = 5, FedAvg flattens out at 1.944 while the optimum is 2.3. What is the single most reliable fix if you must keep that exact data split?
options: Raise the client fraction C so more clients report each round
Train for ten times as many rounds at E = 5
Do less local work per round (smaller E) or correct the local gradients, which both reduce drift
Increase the local learning rate so clients get closer to their local optima
blocks.explain: 1.944 is a fixed point, so more rounds change nothing, and all three clients already report every round so C is irrelevant here. Getting closer to the local optima makes the drift worse: that is the E tending to infinity limit of 1.667. Reducing local work or correcting the local direction (FedProx, SCAFFOLD) attacks the actual cause.

blocks.question: A colleague says FedAvg with E = 5 was fine on their IID benchmark, so the non-IID result must be a bug. What is the right response?
options: They are right: FedAvg is split-independent by construction
With IID clients every local optimum equals the global one, so there is nothing to drift toward; the skew is what creates the bias
The IID result must also be biased, just less visibly
Drift only appears when clients have different sample counts
blocks.explain: In our IID split every client has curvature 10/3 and local optimum 2.3, so the fixed point is 2.3 for any E and larger E is pure speedup. Unequal sample counts alone are harmless, since FedAvg already weights by n_k; what hurts is local objectives that disagree with the pooled one.

blocks.question: Why is SCAFFOLD usually described as a better fit for cross-silo than for cross-device federated learning?
options: It requires every client to keep its control variate across rounds and doubles the upload, while phones are stateless and rarely selected twice
It needs a GPU on every client
Its server update is incompatible with weighted averaging
It only converges when every client holds IID data
blocks.explain: The variate c_i is per-client state carried from one participation to the next, and the upload carries a model delta plus a variate delta. Ten hospitals that join every round can do both; a phone that participates once in a training run never gets to use its variate.

lessons.title: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum

blocks.md:
In a production cross-device system a client is eligible only when it is idle, charging and on an unmetered network such as wifi. Tens of thousands of devices may announce availability in a window, and the server invites typically a few hundred of them to a round.

A round then has three phases. **Selection**: eligible devices check in on a bidirectional stream and the server picks a subset; the phase ends when a participant goal count is reached or a timeout fires. **Configuration**: the server sends the training plan and the current model. **Reporting**: the server waits for updates, aggregates them as they arrive, and closes the round if enough devices reported in time. If not enough did, the round is abandoned and nothing is applied. That minimum number of reports is the round's quorum, a word borrowed from meetings, where a vote only counts if enough members are present.

blocks.title: One round: the server closes on a quorum, not on everyone

scenes.caption: Selection. Eligible devices check in; the server accepts until it has its goal count or the selection timeout fires. Devices it does not want are told when to come back.

Configuration. Each participant downloads the plan and the global model. In bytes download dominates, since the plan is about model-sized and updates compress better; per byte, upload is the slower link (lesson 4).
Local training, and devices are not alike. Device 4 is slow: older hardware, more local examples, or a user who picked the phone up. The server simply waits with a deadline.
Reporting. Updates arrive and are aggregated online as they come in, so the server never has to store them all. Three of four have reported by t = 135 seconds.
The quorum is met, the round closes, and device 4's upload at t = 175 is rejected: it arrives after the reporting window. In one measured population 22 percent of sessions ended exactly this way.

blocks.md:
The operational numbers from a production deployment make the design concrete.

- Between 6 and 10 percent of selected devices drop out per round (computation errors, network failures, or losing eligibility because the user picked up the phone), so the server selects about **130 percent** of the target count. Target 100, invite 130, expect 117 to 122 alive, close the round at 100 and abort the extra.
- Of on-device training sessions: 75 percent completed and were accepted, 22 percent completed but were rejected because they reported after the window closed, 2 percent were interrupted before finishing.
- The system handled roughly 10 million daily active devices with up to 10000 participating simultaneously, and a 4x difference between daytime and nighttime participation for a US-centric population.
- For the next-word model, a round took two to three minutes and 3000 rounds took 5 days.

Partial participation interacts badly with skew, which you can see on our three-client problem. Suppose the server samples one client per round instead of all three, round robin, with $E = 5$. The weighting does nothing now, because the only reporting client gets weight $n_k/m_t = 1$, so the global model is dragged to whichever client happened to be picked.

blocks.title: Global model after each round: all clients versus one per round

scenes.caption: All three clients every round, E = 5. Monotone and boring: it is within 0.01 of its (biased) fixed point 1.9439 by round 5 and stays there.
One client per round, cycling A, C, B. The model is yanked to 3.0 whenever client C is picked and back down when A is. With E = 5 the server is effectively adopting one client's local answer.

blocks.md:
Real systems avoid that oscillation by sampling hundreds of clients per round, so the round's data distribution is close to the population's, and by keeping the client fraction modest ($C = 0.1$ in the original experiments; a few hundred devices per round was found sufficient in production, with diminishing returns beyond that). It is averaging over clients within a round, not across rounds, that stabilizes the update.

The server also paces check-ins. A flow-control mechanism tells rejected devices when to reconnect, which both avoids a thundering herd for large populations and gathers enough simultaneous devices for small ones. A thundering herd is many clients retrying at the same moment and swamping the server; giving each device its own time to come back spreads that load out.

A federated round is a **rendezvous with a quorum**, not a barrier over all clients. The server waits for a minimum percentage of a goal count within a time window, aggregates whoever made it, ignores the stragglers, and abandons the round if too few arrive.

blocks.question: You need 200 reporting devices per round and measure an 8 percent dropout rate. How many should you invite, and what happens to the extras?
options: Exactly 200, and retry the ones that fail inside the same round
About 260 (130 percent), closing the round once 200 have reported and aborting the rest
As many as check in, aggregating every update that ever arrives
400, so that a full round survives even if half the devices vanish
blocks.explain: Over-selecting by about 130 percent is the deployed practice: it absorbs the 6 to 10 percent that drop out and lets the slowest tail be discarded. The round closes on the quorum, and the surplus tail gets aborted, which is why 22 percent of sessions in the measured population finished training but had their result rejected.

blocks.question: Why does sampling only one client per round make the oscillation above so violent, while sampling 300 clients per round does not?
options: A single client's update is noisier, but the drift direction is unaffected
FedAvg cannot weight a single client correctly
The oscillation is a learning-rate artifact that more clients happen to damp
With one client the round's data distribution is that client's distribution, while 300 clients approximate the population
blocks.explain: The weighted average is a sample estimate of the population objective. With one skewed client per round, the server is optimizing that client's objective for a whole round; with hundreds, the mixture is close to the population and the averaging inside the round smooths the local optima together. FedAvg does weight one client correctly: the weight is 1.

lessons.title: One model is not enough: personalization, async and vertical FL

blocks.md:
So far the goal was one global model, and lesson 5 treated anything other than 2.3 as an error. Sometimes the clients disagree because they really want different answers. Mansour and colleagues at Google open their personalization paper with a keyboard prompt, *I live in the state of*: one global model must predict the same state for every user, which is wrong for most of them.

The usual answer keeps the global model and adds a **personalized** model per client. The cheapest form is local fine-tuning: take the global model and run a few local steps on the client's own data. Mansour et al. ([2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.10619)) analyse three more structured ways to sit between a purely local and a purely global model.

- **User clustering**: group clients and train one model per cluster. Same privacy as one global model, but $q$ clusters cost $q$ times the communication.
- **Data interpolation**: train on a weighted mix of the client's data and the global data, choosing the mix by cross-validation. The paper calls out its communication cost and data exposure as non-trivial, and gives an algorithm (DAPPER) that keeps the overhead small.
- **Model interpolation**: train a global model and a local one and predict with $\lambda h_{\text{local}} + (1 - \lambda) h_{\text{global}}$. Same communication and security as training a single model.

A local model alone generalizes badly: the authors note that a keyboard user has on the order of hundreds of examples, while the model class's complexity (its pseudo-dimension) is in the millions.

**Ditto** (Li, Hu, Beirami and Smith, 2021) makes the in-between explicit. Every client trains a personal model $v_k$ on its own loss plus a penalty for straying from the global optimum $w^*$, which is trained by ordinary FedAvg. The penalty has FedProx's shape, but its job is different: FedProx's term shapes the one shared model, while Ditto's produces a second model that never leaves the client.

blocks.tex: \min_{v_k}\; h_k(v_k; w^*) = F_k(v_k) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert v_k - w^* \rVert^2 \quad\text{s.t.}\quad w^* \in \arg\min_w \sum_k p_k F_k(w)
blocks.caption: Ditto's objective. lambda = 0 gives purely local training; lambda growing without bound recovers the global model.

blocks.md:
On our toy the personal optimum has a closed form. Client $k$'s loss is $\frac{a_k}{2}(v - \mu_k)^2$, so setting the derivative of $h_k$ to zero gives $v_k = (a_k\mu_k + \lambda w^*)/(a_k + \lambda)$ with $w^* = 2.3$: a mix of the client's own answer and the global one, weighted by the client's curvature against $\lambda$.

- $\lambda = 0$: 1, 2, 3, each client's own optimum.
- $\lambda = 1$: 1.6500, 2.0600, 2.9300.
- $\lambda = 10$: 2.1818, 2.2143, 2.6316.

Client C, the steepest ($a = 9$), holds on to its own answer longest; client A ($a = 1$) gives way first.

blocks.title: Ditto's personal models on our three clients as lambda grows

scenes.caption: The global model every client receives: 2.3. Client A wants 1, B wants 2, C wants 3.
Client A. At lambda = 1 it is already at 1.65, halfway, because its own loss is shallow (a = 1) and the penalty easily outweighs it.
All three. At lambda = 10 client C still sits at 2.63: its steep local loss (a = 9) resists the pull. Each client can tune its own lambda on local validation data.

blocks.question: Under Ditto with lambda = 1 on our toy, which client's personal model ends closest to its own local optimum?
options: Client A, because it holds the most data
All three move the same distance, since lambda is shared
Client C, because its steep local loss (a = 9) outweighs the penalty
Client B, because its optimum 2 is nearest to 2.3
blocks.explain: v_k = (a_k mu_k + lambda w*)/(a_k + lambda). At lambda = 1, C sits at 2.93, only 0.07 from its optimum 3, while A sits at 1.65, 0.65 from its optimum 1. Sample count does not enter the personal objective at all; curvature does.

blocks.md:
Personalization changes the goal. **Asynchronous** FL changes the round. Lesson 6's synchronous round waits for a quorum, so the number of clients training at once, the *concurrency*, equals the cohort size. Nguyen and colleagues at Meta found that synchronous FL gives diminishing returns beyond a few hundred clients per round, like large-batch training. Fully asynchronous FL, which applies each update the moment it arrives, scales further but breaks secure aggregation (lesson 9: a protocol that lets the server learn only the sum of many updates): there is no sum to hide an individual update in.

**FedBuff** (buffered asynchronous aggregation, 2022) sits between the two. Clients start and finish whenever they are available; the server adds arriving updates into a buffer and takes a step after every $K$ of them ($K = 10$ worked across their benchmarks). An update computed on an older model is **stale**: its staleness $\tau$ is the number of server steps since that model, and FedBuff down-weights it by $1/\sqrt{1 + \tau}$.

blocks.title: FedBuff with a buffer of K = 2 updates

scenes.caption: No rounds. Four clients start training on model version v0 whenever they become available, at 0, 0, 5 and 10 seconds. Nobody waits for anybody.
Clients 1 and 2 report at 30 and 45 s. The buffer holds K = 2, so the server steps to v1. Both updates were computed on the current version: staleness 0, weight 1.
Clients 3 and 4 report at 60 and 80 s, trained on v0 while the server is at v1: staleness 1, weight 1/sqrt(2) = 0.71 each. The buffer fills again and the server steps to v2.

blocks.md: Because every server step sums $K > 1$ updates, secure aggregation (inside a trusted execution environment, an isolated hardware enclave whose code the operator cannot inspect or alter, or a cryptographic protocol) still hides individuals, and the authors pair FedBuff with DP-FTRL (differentially private follow-the-regularized-leader), the private training method of lesson 9 that does not need random client sampling. They report FedBuff 3.3x more efficient than synchronous FL (FedAvgM) and up to 2.5x more efficient than fully asynchronous FL.

The last change is to what each party holds. Everything so far is **horizontal** FL: clients share the feature space and hold different samples (different phones, same kind of typing data). In **vertical** FL the parties hold the *same* people but *different features*: a bank and a retailer with overlapping customers, or, in the survey by Liu and colleagues, WeBank working with an invoice agency on risk models. The party holding the labels is the *active* party; the others are *passive*.

Training has two steps. First **entity alignment**: find the shared customer IDs without revealing the rest, using private set intersection, a protocol that reveals only the IDs both lists share (optional depth: course *Privacy engineering*, lesson 14). Then each party runs its own sub-model on its own columns and sends the output to the active party, which computes the loss and sends back the gradient with respect to each output, so each party can update its own sub-model. Models never move; intermediate results do, and every party keeps its own model, so predictions also need all parties.

blocks.title: Vertical FL: same customers, different columns

scenes.caption: Entity alignment: the two parties find their shared customers with private set intersection, learning nothing about customers only the other one has. Simplified: each side blinds its hashed IDs with a secret key, because plain hashes can be inverted.
Forward pass for a batch of shared customers: each party runs its own sub-model on its own columns, and only the outputs H1 and H2 cross the boundary to the active party.
Backward pass: the active party computes the loss and sends each party the gradient of the loss with respect to its output. The bank updates G1 without ever seeing the retailer's labels or columns.

blocks.question: Two banks share most of their customers. One holds transaction histories and default labels, the other holds savings and mortgage data for the same people. Which setting fits?
options: Cross-device horizontal FedAvg, one client per customer
Horizontal cross-silo FedAvg, one client per bank
Ditto, so each bank gets a personalized model
Vertical FL: align shared customers privately, then exchange intermediate outputs and gradients
blocks.explain: Same samples, different features is the definition of vertical FL. Horizontal FedAvg averages models over clients that hold the same kind of columns, which these banks do not. Personalization addresses clients that want different answers on the same features.

lessons.title: Threats: what updates leak and how clients poison the model

blocks.md:
Two threats motivate everything in the next lesson. The server may learn too much from an update, and a client may send an update designed to harm the model.

Start with leakage on the smallest network there is: one linear layer $z = Wx + b$ with three inputs and two outputs, and squared loss $\frac{1}{2}\lVert z - y\rVert^2$. Let $\delta = z - y$ be the output error. The chain rule gives $\partial L/\partial W = \delta x^{\top}$ (row $i$ is $\delta_i$ times the input) and $\partial L/\partial b = \delta$. So dividing row $i$ of the weight gradient by entry $i$ of the bias gradient returns the private input $x$ exactly, with no optimization at all.

blocks.tex: \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = \delta\, x^{\top}, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \delta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \frac{(\partial L/\partial W)_{i,:}}{(\partial L/\partial b)_i}\ \text{ for any } i \text{ with } \delta_i \neq 0
blocks.caption: Input recovery from one linear layer's gradient. One local SGD step sends -eta times both gradients, and the ratio is unchanged, so the update leaks the input just as well.

blocks.title: Reading the private input out of a gradient

scenes.caption: The server sees only gradients. Here W = [[0.2, -0.1, 0.3], [0, 0.4, -0.2]], b = (0.1, -0.3), target y = (1, 0); the client's input is hidden.
The bias gradient is the output error itself: dL/db = (-0.1, -1.1). The client also sends this.
Divide row 0 by -0.1: (0.5, -1, 2). Divide row 1 by -1.1: the same (0.5, -1, 2). Both rows are the input scaled by one error each.
And that is the private input, exactly. Simplified: a batch of several inputs mixes their rows, which is why larger batches leak less cleanly.

blocks.md:
Deep networks are harder only in degree. Geiping and colleagues (2020) proved that the input to any fully connected layer with a bias can be reconstructed analytically like this, which already exposes the features fed into a classifier's last layers. For convolutional inputs, attacks optimize instead: **Deep Leakage from Gradients** (Zhu, Liu and Han, 2019) starts from random dummy data and labels and adjusts them until their gradient matches the observed one, recovering CIFAR images pixel by pixel. More examples per gradient make it slower: on ResNet-20 (a 20-layer convolutional image classifier) it needed 270 iterations for a batch of 1 and 2711 for a batch of 8.

*Inverting Gradients* (Geiping et al.) matched gradient direction (cosine similarity) instead, and attacked FedAvg-style updates directly. One image survived 100 local gradient steps with reconstruction quality unimpeded, and 5 local epochs were no harder to invert than 1. Averaging over 100 images made most reconstructions unrecognizable, but some were still recognizable.

Many local steps are not a privacy defense: in the Inverting Gradients experiments more local epochs did not make reconstruction harder. More examples per update did make it harder, but not safe. The paper's conclusion is that provable differential privacy is the only way to guarantee security.

Now the second threat. Bagdasaryan and colleagues (2020) assume an attacker who controls one or more participants: their data, their training procedure and hyperparameters, and the weights they submit. Their **model replacement** attack targets the aggregation rule itself. If the server computes $G_{t+1} = G_t + \frac{\eta}{n}\sum_i (L_i - G_t)$ over $n$ clients, and near convergence the honest deviations $L_i - G_t$ roughly cancel, then an attacker who submits $G_t + \gamma(X - G_t)$ with $\gamma = n/\eta$ makes the new global model approximately $X$, any model of its choosing. In their experiments a single attacker selected for a single round gave the joint model 100 percent accuracy on the backdoor task (a hidden behaviour the attacker chose, such as labelling images with a certain feature as a chosen class, while the main task still looks normal).

blocks.prompt: Back to our three clients, converged at w = 2.3 with E = 1. Honest A and B return 2.17 and 2.18. Client C carries weight 1/6 and wants the global model at X = 0, so it submits 2.3 + 6 x (0 - 2.3) = -11.5. What is the new global model?
blocks.reveal: 0.5 x 2.17 + (1/3) x 2.18 + (1/6) x (-11.5) = 1.085 + 0.727 - 1.917 = **-0.105**. One client in three, holding a sixth of the data, moved the model from 2.3 to within 0.105 of its target in one round. The leftover 0.105 is exactly the honest deviations that did not cancel (they are -0.13 and -0.12 from 2.3). An honest C would have sent 2.93 and the model would have stayed at 2.3.

blocks.md:
Defenses replace the weighted mean with something an outlier cannot drag far. Yin and colleagues (2018) analysed two coordinate-wise rules: the **median** of each coordinate across clients, and the **$\beta$-trimmed mean**, which drops the largest and smallest $\beta$ fraction of each coordinate before averaging. **Krum** (Blanchard and colleagues, [2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.02757)) picks one whole update: for each update it sums the squared distances to its $n - f - 2$ nearest neighbours, where $f$ is the number of attackers to tolerate (it needs $2f + 2 < n$), and keeps the update with the smallest sum. **Norm clipping** is the cheapest: scale every update down to length at most $S$ before averaging, which bounds what any one client can do.

The figure uses five scalar updates, one from an attacker: 1.0, 1.2, 0.8, 1.1 and 9.0.

blocks.title: Five updates, one attacker, and what each aggregator returns

scenes.caption: Four honest updates near 1 and one attacker at 9.0.
The plain mean is 2.62: one update in five more than doubled the honest consensus.
Median 1.1. Trimmed mean with beta = 0.2 drops one value from each end (0.8 and 9.0) and averages the rest: 1.1. The attacker's value no longer matters.
Krum with f = 1 sums squared distances to each update's 2 nearest neighbours: 0.05, 0.05, 0.13, 0.02 and 123.25. Client 4's update (1.1) has the smallest score and is chosen.
Clipping to length 2 turns 9.0 into 2.0, and the mean becomes 1.22. Cheaper, and works with any averaging, but a clipped attacker still pulls a little every round.

blocks.md:
These defenses collide with the privacy defense of the next lesson. Secure aggregation lets the server see only the sum, so it cannot compute a median, run Krum, or look for an outlier at all; Bagdasaryan et al. note that with secure aggregation there is no way to detect a malicious model, nor who sent it. The field survey by Kairouz, McMahan and colleagues lists this as an open tension. Clipping can be asked of each client, but under secure aggregation the server cannot check that a malicious client complied; range proofs can enforce it, and making them efficient is still active research. The geometric median has been approximated with a handful of secure aggregation calls, but which aggregators can run under secure aggregation is not known in general.

Personalization helps too: Ditto's authors report that personal models resist poisoning better than a single corrupted global model.

Updates leak inputs (exactly, for a fully connected layer), and a single client can replace the global model in one round by scaling its update by n/eta. Robust aggregators need to see individual updates; secure aggregation exists to hide them. Pick your threat model before you pick your aggregator.

blocks.question: A project aggregates with the coordinate-wise median to resist poisoned clients. The privacy team now wants secure aggregation as well (next lesson: each client adds random masks that cancel only in the sum). What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the median of masked updates equals the masked median
The server only receives masked values whose sum is meaningful, so it cannot take a per-coordinate median of individual updates
Secure aggregation requires FedProx, not a median
Secure aggregation removes the attacker's update automatically, so the median is redundant
blocks.explain: Masking is built so that only the sum is revealed: each masked upload looks uniformly random, and the masks cancel only when all of them are added. A median is not a sum, so it cannot be computed from that output. This is the privacy and robustness tension in the FL survey.

blocks.question: An auditor argues that FedAvg's 5 local epochs per round make client updates safe to share in the clear. Based on the Inverting Gradients experiments, what is the best reply?
options: Correct: after 5 epochs the update no longer depends on individual examples
Correct only for convolutional networks
Wrong: 5 local epochs were no harder to invert than 1; only more images per update made reconstruction harder, and not safe
Wrong, because local epochs make updates larger and therefore easier to invert
blocks.explain: Geiping et al. found single-image reconstructions unimpeded even after 100 local steps, and their 8-image experiments were no harder at 5 epochs than at 1. Averaging over more images lowered quality, but some images from a batch of 100 were still recognizable. Formal protection needs differential privacy.

lessons.title: What the server sees: secure aggregation and differential privacy

blocks.md:
Keeping raw data on the device is not the same as keeping it private. A plain FedAvg server receives one parameter vector per client per round, and lesson 8 showed what that update can carry: the exact input of a fully connected layer, and recognizable images from deep networks. For a language model it can carry rare strings nearly verbatim.

Two defenses attack two different problems. **Secure aggregation** stops the server from seeing any individual update while still letting it compute the sum. The usual threat model is an honest-but-curious server: it runs the protocol exactly as specified but tries to learn whatever it can from the messages it receives. **Differential privacy** limits what the aggregate itself reveals about any one contributor. They compose, and neither replaces the other.

The course *Privacy engineering* (optional, not a prerequisite) teaches the definition of differential privacy (its lesson 8), its trust models (lesson 10) and secure aggregation in general (lesson 15); this lesson teaches them from scratch, only as far as federated training needs.

Secure aggregation is built from pairwise masks. Every pair of users $u$ and $v$ agrees on two random vectors, $s_{u,v}$ and $s_{v,u}$, and forms $p_{u,v} = s_{u,v} - s_{v,u} \bmod R$, which has the property $p_{u,v} = -p_{v,u}$. Swapping $u$ and $v$ flips the sign, which is why the two masks cancel. $R$ is a fixed integer modulus: all arithmetic wraps around at $R$ like a clock, so adding a uniformly random mask mod $R$ gives a result that is itself uniformly random and reveals nothing about the value. Each user adds all its pairwise masks to its own value and uploads the result. Individually those uploads look uniformly random; summed, every mask cancels against its partner. (This is the 2016 paper's formulation; the later full paper, and the course *Privacy engineering*, use one shared value per pair, added by the lower id and subtracted by the higher. The effect is the same.)

blocks.tex: y_u = x_u + b_u + \sum_{v} p_{u,v} \bmod R, \qquad p_{u,v} = -p_{v,u} \;\Longrightarrow\; \sum_u y_u = \sum_u x_u \bmod R
blocks.caption: The masking identity, with b_u an extra per-user mask explained below. Updates are mapped into integers mod R by clipping, scaling and quantizing them first.

blocks.title: Three users, one scalar each, mod 100

scenes.caption: Each pair exchanges two random seeds over an authenticated channel (relayed by the server but encrypted end to end). A and B derive p_AB = 47 and p_BA = 53, which sum to 100, that is 0 mod 100.

The private values are 12, 30 and 55. Masks are 11, 97 and 92, so the uploads are 23, 27 and 47. Not one of those three numbers is close to the value it hides, and the server cannot tell them from random.
The true sum is 12 + 30 + 55 = 97. The server learned the sum and nothing else: no individual value, and no way to subtract one user out. Simplified: this figure uses the pairwise masks only.

Now user C drops out before uploading. Its masks no longer cancel, so the sum is garbage. Recovery: each user also secret-shared its seeds, so the server can ask the survivors to reconstruct C's masks.

blocks.md: Dropout recovery is where the protocol earns the word practical. Each user splits its secrets with a $(t, n)$ threshold scheme (Shamir sharing) with $t > n/2$, so any $t$ survivors can reconstruct a dropped user's masks and the sum still comes out. A $(t, n)$ threshold scheme splits a secret into $n$ shares so that any $t$ of them rebuild it and fewer than $t$ reveal nothing. Shamir's version, from Adi Shamir in 1979, hides the secret as the constant term of a random polynomial of degree $t - 1$ and hands each user one point on it: $t$ points pin down such a polynomial exactly, while $t - 1$ points fit every possible constant equally well.

That alone would break privacy: a server could falsely declare a live user dropped and ask for its masks. Hence the second, individual mask $b_u$. In the unmasking round the server must choose, per user, either the shares of that user's pairwise seeds (if it claims the user dropped) or the shares of $b_u$ (if the user survived), and an honest survivor never gives both. So every value stays hidden behind one mask or the other. The protocol tolerates up to one third of users failing to complete it, and costs about 1.73x the bytes of sending data in the clear for 16-bit input values, $2^{10}$ users and $2^{20}$-dimensional vectors.

Secure aggregation hides *who contributed what*. It does not make the result safe to publish: the sum of 100 updates can still reveal a rare phrase typed by one user. For that you need noise, and a budget that accounts for every round you release.

Differentially private federated averaging makes four changes to FedAvg: select users by independent sampling with probability $q$ rather than taking a fixed count, clip each user's update so its L2 norm is at most $S$ (flat, or per layer), form the bounded-sensitivity weighted average, and add Gaussian noise to that average. The L2 norm is the vector's ordinary Euclidean length. Sensitivity is the most that adding or removing one user can change the average; clipping every update to length $S$ (and capping each user's weight) bounds it, and Gaussian noise scaled to that bound is what hides any single user.

The result is reported as an $(\epsilon, \delta)$ guarantee: $\epsilon$ bounds how much the distribution over released models can shift when one user is added or removed, so a smaller $\epsilon$ is a stronger promise, and $\delta$ is the small probability that the bound fails. Privacy loss across rounds is tracked with the moments accountant, bookkeeping borrowed from differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD), that composes those per-round bounds into one $\epsilon$. The unit of protection is the **user**, not the example: the guarantee is about datasets that differ by one user's entire contribution.

The DP-SGD method (Abadi and colleagues, 2016) trains an ordinary model privately by clipping and noising per-example gradients. Simply adding up each round's $\epsilon$ would grow linearly with the number of rounds; the moments accountant instead tracks bounds on the moments of the privacy loss (how much more likely an output is with one user than without), which add across rounds and convert to one $\epsilon$ that grows far more slowly. Random sampling helps too: a user who is in a round only with probability $q$ has a per-round cost that shrinks roughly in proportion to $q$, called privacy amplification by sampling. In the formula below, $\Delta_k$ is user $k$'s update (its trained model minus the broadcast one), $w_k$ is that user's averaging weight (not a model), $W$ is the sum of all weights, $z$ is the noise multiplier and $\sigma$ the noise standard deviation.

blocks.caption: Clip, then average, then noise. Simplified: the paper defines the sensitivity S-tilde of the exact weighted-average estimator and sets the noise relative to it, and the accountant needs the random user sampling to get amplification.

blocks.md:
A worked round, with numbers from a script. Four sampled users send 2-D updates (3, 4), (0.6, 0.8), (0, -1.5) and (6, -8), with L2 norms 5, 1, 1.5 and 10. Clip at $S = 2$: the first is scaled by 0.4 to (1.2, 1.6), the last by 0.2 to (1.2, -1.6), and the two short ones pass unchanged.

Every user has weight 1, and the sampling rate $q$ is chosen so that $qW = 4$ users are expected per round. The fixed-denominator average is the clipped sum (3.0, -0.7) divided by 4, giving (0.75, -0.175). Its sensitivity is $S/(qW) = 0.5$: adding or removing one user moves it by at most 0.5. With noise multiplier $z = 1$ the server adds Gaussian noise with $\sigma = 0.5$ to each coordinate. One draw (seed 0) released (0.813, -0.241). Without clipping, the average would have been (2.4, -1.175), dominated by the one huge update.

blocks.title: Clip, average, add noise: one DP-FedAvg round

scenes.caption: Four sampled updates, one per column, and their lengths. The fourth is ten times the second: without a bound, one user can dominate the average and stand out in it.
Clip to S = 2: scale factors 0.4, 1, 1 and 0.2. Directions are kept; only lengths above 2 shrink.
Clipped updates: (1.2, 1.6), (0.6, 0.8), (0, -1.5), (1.2, -1.6). No single user can now move the sum by more than length 2, so the average over qW = 4 moves by at most 0.5.
Average (0.75, -0.175) plus Gaussian noise with sigma = z x 0.5 = 0.5 per coordinate gives (0.813, -0.241) for one draw. Noise as large as the signal: four users is far too few.

blocks.md: The same arithmetic at the paper's scale: with $S = 20$ and 100 expected users per round, the sensitivity is 0.2, and noise of $\sigma = 0.2$ destroys accuracy. With $S = 15$ and 1250 expected users, the sensitivity is 0.012, $\sigma = 0.012$, and the moments accountant gives $(1.97, 10^{-9})$-DP after 3000 rounds. The noise on the clipped sum is fixed at $z S$; dividing by $qW$ is what makes it small relative to the average.

blocks.title: Privacy budget after 5000 rounds of the same LSTM

scenes.caption: Epsilon on a dataset of 763430 users, at delta = 1e-9, with 5000, 1667 and 1250 users expected per round. More noise buys a smaller epsilon. The no-noise run has no guarantee at all (epsilon unbounded), so its bar is drawn at zero.
The same three configurations on a population of 1e8 users: epsilon 1.152, 0.991 and 0.987. Nothing about the noise changed. Privacy got cheaper purely because each user is one of far more.

blocks.md:
And the utility cost, measured as top-1 next-word accuracy after 5000 rounds on the 763430-user dataset: 17.62 percent with no noise, 17.49 percent at epsilon 4.63, 17.04 percent at epsilon 2.31, 16.33 percent at epsilon 2.04. Top-1 accuracy is the share of positions where the model's single highest-scoring guess for the next word is the right word.

So the tradeoff is not mainly accuracy, it is compute. The non-private baseline reached 17.5 percent using 100 users per round; matching that accuracy with a (4.6, 1e-9) guarantee needed about 5000 users per round, roughly 60x more work, because larger noise has to be averaged over more contributions. The paper's summary is that with enough users, privacy costs computation rather than utility.

**Who adds the noise.** DP-FedAvg as described is *central* DP: the server is trusted to add the noise honestly, and it sees the noise-free aggregate first. Secure aggregation removes the individual updates from its view but not the clean sum. In *distributed* DP (what the course *Privacy engineering* files under its secure computation trust model), each client adds a share of the noise before secure aggregation, designed so that the sum carries the full noise; the server then never sees an un-noised result. *Local* DP has each client add enough noise to protect itself alone, which costs far more accuracy for the same $\epsilon$.
