**What production does.** Amplification by sampling assumes each round's users are drawn uniformly at random, but a real system can only pick from devices that happen to be idle, charging and on wifi. DP-FTRL (Kairouz and colleagues, [2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00039)) avoids that assumption: it adds correlated noise to running sums of the updates through a binary tree (tree aggregation). Gboard trained more than twenty language models with it, with guarantees between 0.2 and 2 in $\rho$-zCDP (zero-concentrated DP, another accounting unit; smaller $\rho$ is stronger), two of them also under secure aggregation. As of Xu et al. (2023), all of Gboard's next-word neural language models carry DP guarantees.

Clip each user's update to bound sensitivity, divide by the expected number of users, add noise scaled to that bound, and account for every round. More users per round is what makes the noise affordable. Secure aggregation hides individuals from the server; DP hides individuals from everyone who sees the model.

blocks.question: Under secure aggregation with 500 clients in a round, what does an honest-but-curious server learn?
options: Each client's update, but only in encrypted form it cannot use
The sum of the 500 masked updates, from which it can subtract any client it chooses
Nothing at all, including the sum, until a trusted third party decrypts it
The sum of the 500 updates and nothing about any individual update
blocks.explain: The functionality is exactly summation: the server learns the sum and no individual contribution. It cannot subtract one client out, because each client's value is covered by masks that only cancel in the full sum, and the per-user mask b_u blocks the attack of falsely declaring a live client dropped.

blocks.question: Your DP federated run has far worse accuracy than the non-private baseline at the same epsilon. Which change most directly fixes it, according to the published results?
options: Sample many more users per round, so the same noise is averaged over more clipped updates
Lower the clipping norm S, so each update contributes less
Reduce the number of rounds, since every round spends privacy budget
Switch from user-level to example-level accounting and report that instead
blocks.explain: Noise is added once per round to the average, so more users per round shrinks its relative size at fixed epsilon: matching the baseline needed about 5000 users per round instead of 100, roughly 60x the compute. Lowering S adds clipping bias, and with large populations extra rounds cost very little budget (epsilon moved from 0.84 to 0.88 over a million rounds at 1e9 users).

blocks.question: Why did Gboard's production training move from DP-FedAvg's accounting to DP-FTRL?
options: DP-FTRL needs no clipping
DP-FTRL does not add noise, so accuracy is higher
Secure aggregation cannot be used with DP-FedAvg
DP-FedAvg's best guarantees rely on amplification by sampling, which needs uniformly random client selection that a device fleet cannot guarantee
blocks.explain: Devices are eligible only when idle, charging and on an unmetered network, so the server cannot sample users uniformly, and the sampling-based accountant's assumption breaks. DP-FTRL adds tree-correlated noise to prefix sums of updates and gets its guarantee from bounding how often and how close together a client participates.

lessons.title: Build it: a non-IID federated run in Flower, end to end

blocks.md: Flower is an open-source Python framework for federated learning. Flower splits a federated system into a **ServerApp** holding a *strategy* (who is selected, how updates are combined) and a **ClientApp** holding local training. Named strategies ship with it, including FedAvg, FedProx, FedAdam, FedAvgM and FedMedian, so the choices from this course are constructor arguments rather than code. FedAdam and FedAvgM are the server optimizers of lesson 4; FedMedian, FedTrimmedAvg and Krum are the robust aggregators of lesson 8; and Flower also ships differential privacy wrappers and a secure aggregation workflow. This lesson uses three of these strategies on a real non-IID split and measures what happens.

Its simulation runtime (built on Ray) runs many virtual clients, called SuperNodes, on one machine: you set how many with a federation config and how much CPU or GPU each ClientApp gets, and the maximum parallelism is whichever of those limits binds first. Ray is an open-source library for running Python tasks in parallel across processes and machines, and Flower uses it to schedule the virtual clients. The ClientApp objects are the same ones the deployment runtime uses, where a long-lived SuperLink coordinates SuperNodes on real devices ([architecture](https://flower.ai/docs/framework/explanation-flower-architecture.html)). The Flower paper reports experiments up to 15 million clients in client-population size using a pair of high-end GPUs.

The benchmark recipe most papers use for label skew comes from Hsu, Qi and Brown (2019): each client draws its label mix from a **Dirichlet distribution** with concentration $\alpha$, a distribution over probability vectors. Large $\alpha$ gives every client nearly the population's mix; as $\alpha \to 0$ each client holds only one class. It replaces the two-shards-per-client split of lesson 3 with one dial.

The run: MNIST's 60000 training images over 50 SuperNodes, split by Flower Datasets' `DirichletPartitioner` with $\alpha = 100$ (near-IID) and $\alpha = 0.1$ (highly skewed), `min_partition_size=20` and `seed=42`. Each client keeps 80 percent of its partition for training and holds out 20 percent for federated evaluation. Sizes at $\alpha = 100$ ranged from 1125 to 1277 images; at $\alpha = 0.1$ from 25 to 4329.

scenes.caption: alpha = 100: every client holds every digit in nearly equal numbers (client 0: 100 to 139 of each). Each client looks like a small copy of MNIST, close to IID.
alpha = 0.1, same seed: client 0 holds mostly 1s, 6s and 7s, client 1 mostly 4s and 0s, and client 2 has 176 images, 156 of them 1s. Most cells are zero or near zero.

# prep.py: partition once with Flower Datasets, save arrays for the clients
from flwr_datasets import FederatedDataset
from flwr_datasets.partitioner import DirichletPartitioner

for alpha in (0.1, 100.0):
    part = DirichletPartitioner(num_partitions=50, partition_by="label",
                                alpha=alpha, min_partition_size=20, seed=42)
    fds = FederatedDataset(dataset="ylecun/mnist", partitioners={"train": part})
    for pid in range(50):
        split = fds.load_partition(pid).train_test_split(test_size=0.2, seed=42)
        # split["train"] trains on the client, split["test"] is its held-out set
        ...  # saved as uint8 arrays in mnist_dir{alpha}.npz
blocks.caption: Partitioning is done once and saved, so each simulated client loads a small array file instead of rebuilding the split on every call. The script also prints the label counts shown above.

blocks.code:
@client.train()
def train(msg: Message, context: Context):
    cfg = msg.content["config"]
    net = Net(); net.load_state_dict(msg.content["arrays"].to_torch_state_dict())
    global_params = [p.detach().clone() for p in net.parameters()]  # w_t, frozen
    mu = float(cfg.get("proximal-mu", 0.0))   # FedProx sends this; FedAvg does not
    trainloader, _ = load_partition(context.node_config["partition-id"], float(cfg["alpha"]))
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=float(cfg["lr"]))
    net.train()
    for _ in range(int(cfg["local-epochs"])):
        for xb, yb in trainloader:
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = F.cross_entropy(net(xb), yb)
            if mu > 0:  # the client-side half of FedProx: (mu/2)||w - w_t||^2
                prox = sum(((p - g) ** 2).sum() for p, g in zip(net.parameters(), global_params))
                loss = loss + (mu / 2) * prox
            loss.backward(); opt.step()
    content = RecordDict({"arrays": ArrayRecord(net.state_dict()),
                          "metrics": MetricRecord({"num-examples": len(trainloader.dataset)})})
    return Message(content=content, reply_to=msg)
blocks.caption: The ClientApp used in every run (Flower 1.44, PyTorch). Net is a small CNN: two 5x5 convolutions with 6 and 16 channels, a 120-unit layer and 10 outputs. Local SGD, learning rate 0.05, batch 32, E = 2 local epochs.

blocks.md: FedProx lives on both sides. Flower's FedProx strategy aggregates exactly like FedAvg and only adds `proximal-mu` to the config it sends; its reference says each client **must** add $\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert w - w^t\rVert^2$ itself. Two traps in copying its PyTorch snippet: it sums the unsquared `.norm(2)` while the formula squares it, and it keeps `global_params` as a `.parameters()` generator, which `zip` exhausts after the first batch. Freeze a list, as above.

blocks.code:
@server.main()
def main(grid: Grid, context: Context):
    torch.manual_seed(0); random.seed(0)        # model init and the sampler RNG
    common = dict(fraction_train=0.2, fraction_evaluate=0.2, min_train_nodes=10,
                  min_evaluate_nodes=10, min_available_nodes=50)
    strategy = {"fedavg": lambda: FedAvg(**common),
                "fedprox": lambda: FedProx(**common, proximal_mu=0.1),
                "fedadam": lambda: FedAdam(**common, eta=0.01, tau=1e-3)}[STRATEGY]()
    result = strategy.start(grid=grid, initial_arrays=ArrayRecord(Net().state_dict()),
                            train_config=ConfigRecord({"lr": 0.05, "local-epochs": 2, "alpha": ALPHA}),
                            evaluate_config=ConfigRecord({"alpha": ALPHA}),
                            num_rounds=30, evaluate_fn=central_eval)   # test set on the server

run_simulation(server_app=server, client_app=client, num_supernodes=50,
               backend_config={"client_resources": {"num_cpus": 2, "num_gpus": 0.0},
                               "init_args": {"num_cpus": 2}})
blocks.caption: The ServerApp: 10 of 50 SuperNodes train each round (C = 0.2), 10 evaluate. FedAdam keeps its default beta_1 = 0.9 and beta_2 = 0.99. Two CPUs for the whole simulation and two per ClientApp, so one client trains at a time.

blocks.md: Two evaluations run every round. **Federated evaluation**: 10 sampled clients test the new global model on their own held-out 20 percent and the strategy averages their accuracies weighted by example count. It measures the model on the data distribution clients actually have, and it is the only option when no central test set exists. **Centralized evaluation**: the server's `evaluate_fn` scores the model on MNIST's 10000 test images, which follow the population's label mix. With skewed clients the two can disagree, and each round's federated number depends on which 10 clients were drawn.

blocks.prompt: Before looking: which costs more on this MNIST CNN, switching from alpha = 100 to alpha = 0.1, or choosing FedAvg instead of FedProx (mu = 0.1) or FedAdam (eta = 0.01) at the same alpha?
blocks.reveal: The split, by far, well beyond run-to-run noise. In the logged runs, centralized test accuracy first reached 95 percent at round 6 for FedAvg at alpha = 100 and at round 15 at alpha = 0.1; the average over the last five rounds fell from 98.3 to 96.3 percent. Between strategies at a fixed alpha, neither method beat FedAvg in these runs: at alpha = 0.1 the 95 percent mark came at rounds 15, 16 and 23 for FedAvg, FedProx and FedAdam. These are single runs with untuned mu and eta, and the same script with the same seeds is not bit-reproducible (a rerun put FedAvg's 95 percent mark at round 11 and FedProx's at 16), so they show how much the data split matters, not which strategy wins.

scenes.caption: Round 1, centralized test accuracy (percent). One round of 2 local epochs on 10 clients: the near-IID runs are already at 74 percent for FedAvg and FedProx; FedAdam's small server step (eta = 0.01) starts slower.
Round 3. The skewed runs (right three bars) trail the near-IID ones by 17 to 33 points: each round's 10 clients see a lopsided label mix.

Round 5. In this draw near-IID FedProx is at 94.5 percent while FedAvg dipped to 89.3 from 94.3 in round 4: centralized accuracy is noisy round to round because a different 10 clients train each time.
Round 10. In this run near-IID FedAvg first crosses 97 percent here. The skewed runs are between 89 and 93.
Round 20. Everything is above 94 percent. The skewed runs climb, but more slowly, and with bigger round-to-round swings.

Round 30, the last. Near-IID: 98.4, 98.3, 98.0. Skewed: 95.6, 95.7, 96.4. One run per configuration, and reruns are not bit-reproducible, so differences of a point between strategies are within the noise.

Rounds to 95 percent centralized accuracy and the mean over rounds 26 to 30, from one logged run per configuration. Round counts are one draw: a rerun of FedAvg at alpha = 0.1 hit 95 percent at round 11, not 15; last-five means moved about half a point.

- alpha = 100. FedAvg: 95 percent at round 6, last-five-round mean 98.3; FedProx: 95 percent at round 6, last-five-round mean 98.2; FedAdam: 95 percent at round 14, last-five-round mean 97.8.
- alpha = 0.1. FedAvg: 95 percent at round 15, last-five-round mean 96.3; FedProx: 95 percent at round 16, last-five-round mean 96.0; FedAdam: 95 percent at round 23, last-five-round mean 96.3.

The federated evaluation agrees in level (FedAvg's final round: 98.3 percent at alpha = 100, 97.0 at 0.1) but jumps more from round to round, because each round tests on a different 10 clients. Each run took about 100 seconds of strategy time on two CPU cores. Why reruns differ: the seeds fix the initial weights and the sampler's random numbers, but every SuperNode gets a fresh random ID at launch, so other partitions get drawn.

Read results like these the way the papers do: several seeds per configuration, a tuned learning rate per strategy (Reddi et al. tune the server rate eta and tau for FedAdam over a grid), and a stated target. With one unrepeatable run per configuration and default knobs, the honest conclusion is the size of the non-IID penalty, not a ranking of algorithms.

The one thing to remember: federated learning is an optimization algorithm shaped by a systems constraint. Every piece (averaging instead of gradient sharing, a quorum instead of a barrier, masks instead of raw updates, noise instead of trust) exists because rounds are expensive, clients are unreliable, and the server is not allowed to look.

blocks.question: A learner swaps `FedAvg(...)` for `FedProx(..., proximal_mu=0.1)` in the ServerApp and leaves the ClientApp from the Flower quickstart untouched. What does the run compute?
options: FedAvg in effect: the server aggregates exactly as FedAvg and sends proximal-mu, which the unchanged client never reads
FedProx: the strategy applies the proximal term when it aggregates
An error, because the client does not accept the proximal-mu key
FedProx with mu applied twice, once on each side
blocks.explain: Flower's FedProx reference says the strategy behaves identically to FedAvg on the server and only puts proximal-mu into the config; each client must add (mu/2)||w - w_t||^2 to its own loss. Unknown config keys are simply ignored, so nothing fails and nothing changes. Both apps have to change.

blocks.question: In one logged FedAvg run at alpha = 0.1, federated evaluation read 96.7 percent in round 16 and 89.3 percent in round 17, while centralized accuracy moved only from 94.1 to 93.9. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Federated evaluation is computed on the training data
The global model oscillates between rounds
Each round samples 10 different clients, whose held-out sets have very different label mixes and sizes, so the federated number is a noisy sample
Centralized evaluation is broken and should be ignored
blocks.explain: With highly skewed clients, how well the global model does depends on which digits a client holds. Sampling 10 of 50 clients per evaluation round makes the weighted average a noisy estimate; the 10000-image central test set is fixed. Look at both, and average federated metrics over several rounds.
